title: DGFT Extends Rice Export Inspection Exemption For Non-EU Europe To April 2027
seo_title: DGFT Eases Rice Export Rules For Europe
meta_description: DGFT's 9 November 2026 notification extends the rice export inspection-certificate exemption for non-EU/UK Europe to 1 April 2027.
case_name: Notification No. 47/2026-27 (DGFT) - Amendment to Export Policy Condition for Basmati and Non-Basmati Rice (HS Code 1006)
citation: DGFT Notification No. 47/2026-27, dated 9 November 2026, issued under Section 3 read with Section 5 of the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992, amending Notification No. 07/2026-27 dated 10 April 2026
body: On 9 November 2026, the Directorate General of Foreign Trade issued Notification No. 47/2026-27, amending the export policy condition that applies to specified Basmati and non-Basmati rice tariff lines falling under HS code 1006 in Schedule 2 of the ITC(HS) Export Policy. The notification modifies an earlier one, Notification No. 07/2026-27 of 10 April 2026, and takes effect immediately, under the power DGFT exercises jointly under Section 3 and Section 5 of the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992.

The underlying scheme requires an exporter sending specified rice to certain European destinations to produce a Certificate of Inspection, issued either by the Export Inspection Council or by one of its Export Inspection Agencies, before the shipment is permitted under the export policy. That requirement stays unchanged for rice bound for the European Union's member states, the United Kingdom, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland, which remain on the list of destinations where the certificate is mandatory.

What the 9 November notification changes is the treatment of the remaining European countries outside that named list. Exporters sending rice to those destinations do not need the Certificate of Inspection, an exemption the April notification had already granted but on a shorter clock. The new notification extends that exemption until 1 April 2027, giving exporters and the inspection agencies that would otherwise certify each shipment a further window before the requirement would reach more destinations.

The distinction between the named destinations and the rest of Europe is not incidental. It lets the government keep inspection oversight tight for the markets that import the largest volumes or apply the most exacting import standards, while sparing exporters and the EIC's own inspection capacity the burden of certifying every rice shipment bound for a smaller European market. An across-the-board certificate requirement would stretch EIC resources over destinations where, on successive extensions of the same relief, the compliance risk has not been treated as justifying it.

This is also not the first time the exemption window for non-listed European destinations has moved. An earlier version of the same relief, as described in reporting on the April notification, ran only until 1 October 2026; the 9 November notification pushes that relief out a further six months. Exporters relying on the exemption would do well to treat each extension as provisional, since DGFT has renewed this relief in increments rather than making it indefinite.

For rice exporters and trading houses working out of ports and inland container depots that serve the Delhi-NCR and Kolkata trade corridors, the immediate effect is continuity: a shipment to a non-listed European country that could move without a Certificate of Inspection yesterday can still move without one today, and will be able to without one until April 2027 unless the policy changes again before then. The notification changes nothing for shipments to the EU, the UK or the other four named destinations, where the certificate stays mandatory regardless of this amendment.

Because the notification operates by amending Schedule 2 export-policy conditions rather than by primary legislation, DGFT can adjust the list of named destinations, the exemption's end date, or the certificate requirement itself again without needing Parliament's intervention, and on this subject it has already done so more than once within the same year. Exporters structuring long-term supply contracts into smaller European markets on the strength of the exemption should factor that possibility into their planning rather than treat the April 2027 date as final.

The inspection certificate itself is not a trivial formality where it does apply. An Export Inspection Agency physically examines a consignment, or a representative sample of it, against quality parameters before issuing the Certificate of Inspection, and a shipment without one cannot clear for a listed destination regardless of what other export documentation the exporter holds. Removing that step for non-listed destinations, even temporarily, cuts out a source of shipment delay for exporters who deal mainly in smaller consignments to markets outside the EU and the UK, where the fixed cost of arranging an inspection can weigh more heavily on a single container than it does on a large bulk shipment bound for an EU port.
why_it_matters: Rice exporters shipping Basmati or non-Basmati rice to Europe need to know which of two regimes applies to their destination: the European Union, the United Kingdom, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland still require a Certificate of Inspection from the Export Inspection Council before export, while shipments to other European countries remain exempt, now until 1 April 2027 rather than the shorter window the April 2026 notification had set. Exporters and freight forwarders handling consignments to smaller European markets should update their documentation checklists and track the next extension rather than assume the exemption is now settled policy.
card_summary: DGFT's 9 November 2026 notification extends, to 1 April 2027, the rice-export inspection-certificate exemption for European destinations outside the EU, UK, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland.
card_tip: Rice exporters to non-EU/UK European markets can skip the Certificate of Inspection until 1 April 2027 under DGFT Notification 47/2026-27; the EU, UK and four other states still require it.
verification_notes: The notification number (47/2026-27), its date (9 November 2026), and its amendment of the earlier Notification No. 07/2026-27 of 10 April 2026 under Section 3 read with Section 5 of the FTDR Act, 1992 are confirmed across World Trade Scanner's direct reproduction of the notification and the Taxscan and TeamLease RegTech reports, all three giving the same notification and base-notification numbers. The list of destinations where the Certificate of Inspection remains mandatory (EU member states, UK, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, Switzerland) and the extension of the exemption for other European destinations to 1 April 2027 are confirmed by Taxscan and TeamLease RegTech independently. The detail that an earlier version of the same exemption had run only to 1 October 2026 is taken from TeamLease RegTech's description of the April 2026 notification and is used here only as background, not as an operative date under the current notification. A corpseed.com report additionally stated the amendment covers six non-Basmati and two Basmati tariff codes; that figure could not be confirmed from a second source in this run and has been left out of the body.
